paras: The attempted lynching of Frank Clark was a manhunt in late July 1903 in which several hundred armed farmers around Kahoka, Clark County, Missouri, hunted Clark, called a "negro" in most reports, vowing to lynch him for an alleged assault on a white girl, Ollie Hess. Wire reports from Farmington, Iowa, said he was surrounded and would soon be lynched, but the man surrounded was someone else and the mobs dispersed without catching him. Arrested in Illinois in September, Clark was convicted at Kahoka and legally hanged there on November 25, 1903, two hours early because officials feared a mob.

Hess, 15 or 17, lived with her widowed mother about two miles west of Kahoka. Clark was described as a jockey who had raced at Kahoka for years, with his home given as Carrollton or Edina, Missouri; the sheriff called him a "dark mulatto" and the Farmington Journal "part negro and part Italian."

Clark was accused of attacking Hess on the road from Medill on the evening of July 25, dragging her into a hollow and cutting her with a knife; the papers described the attack as rape. When word reached Kahoka at 2 a.m. Sunday, fire bells called out what the Farmington Journal called "a mob of 700 heavily armed men." A Keokuk special of July 28 said several hundred farmers were still hunting him and declared he would be lynched when caught, though Hess was by then recovering.

The hunt seized the wrong men. A man surrounded near Medill on Monday, the basis of the wire's report, was found not to be Clark, and a Black man found by bloodhounds at Mt. Sterling, Iowa, was held and released. In Kahoka an armed guard surrounded the house of Henry Miller, a Black resident seen trying to hire a team that night. By July 30 the mobs had dispersed, and sheriffs from Knox County, Missouri, and Appanoose County, Iowa, continued the search with word that they would protect Clark if caught.

After a false arrest at Oklahoma City in August, Galesburg, Illinois, police arrested Clark in mid-September, and he signed a confession there. Sheriff Arnold took him to Palmyra, two counties away, saying that "a mob would surely lynch him" in Clark County. Before the trial, a Kahoka resident warned that anything short of a death sentence might lead neighbors to "take matters into their own hands."

Clark was found guilty and Judge McKee set his execution for November 25. That day officials hanged him two hours before the announced time, fearing a mob would break down the stockade, and the St. Louis Republic reported that the crowd tore boards from it before the drop. No report of any arrest or inquiry concerning the July mob appears in the coverage.

The first-day wire ran in New York, Minneapolis, Louisville and Omaha under headlines such as "Iowa Mob Seeks to Lynch Negro," and the Minneapolis Journal called Clark a "Black Brute." Because of the Farmington dateline these papers placed the hunt in Iowa, and the San Antonio Daily Light reduced it to a line about mobs "pursuing negroes to lynch them for outrages on women." Iowa papers near the scene printed longer accounts; the Ottumwa Courier called Clark "the fiend" who would be "hung to the nearest tree," while later Kahoka reports stressed the county's good name.

The Black press covered the case late and briefly. The American Citizen noted in August that Hess's assailant had been "chased from Missouri by a mob intent upon lynching him." The St. Louis Palladium printed the wire on his arrest and fear of being burned, and the Iowa State Bystander reprinted the sentence report calling him "the confessed ravisher"; none of these papers commented on the mob.

The wire named the girl Gertrude Hess and called her "fatally injured," while Kahoka dispatches named her Ollie and had her recovering within days. Most reports called Clark a "negro," but he said he was "half Mexican and half Indian." The Oskaloosa Herald described the pursuers as a posse of more than 200 under Sheriff Arnold, while Keokuk and Farmington reports called them a mob of several hundred to 700.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Frank Clark
bases: Armed mobs of several hundred farmers hunted Clark for days declaring he would be lynched when caught, but never took him (A15, A16, A17); his later legal execution is a separate matter (A32).

The mob that hunted Clark in July 1903 declared it would lynch him for the alleged assault but did not catch him (A15, A18); he was later tried and hanged by the authorities at Kahoka (A29, A32), so no one was killed illegally by a group.

The wire report (A1, A3), a Keokuk special (A15, A16), the Farmington Journal (A17) and a Des Moines special (A18) independently describe the armed mob hunt, and later Galesburg and Kahoka reports refer back to it (A26, A28).

accounts.label: Wire report (Farmington, Ia.)
accounts.gist: A mob of farmers searching for Clark had surrounded him in a hollow near Medill and he would soon be lynched; the girl was thought fatally injured.

accounts.label: Keokuk and Kahoka specials
accounts.gist: Several hundred farmers were still hunting Clark on July 28 and vowed to lynch him on sight, though Hess was recovering; bloodhounds failed; reward raised.

accounts.label: Farmington Journal, with Hess's interview
accounts.gist: A 700-man armed mob turned out at the fire bells; the man surrounded near Medill was the wrong man, a reported capture at Coffee church was false, and Clark was last seen near Downing and Memphis.

accounts.label: Des Moines special
accounts.gist: The mobs had dispersed by July 30, leaving the search to Iowa and Missouri officers who would protect Clark if caught.

accounts.label: Sheriff's and Galesburg accounts
accounts.gist: Clark was arrested at Galesburg, confessed, and was taken to Palmyra because the sheriff said a mob would lynch him in Clark County.

accounts.label: Black-press briefs
accounts.gist: The American Citizen noted the mob chase; the Palladium and Bystander reprinted wire news of the arrest and sentence.

framing.detail: First-day headlines 'Iowa Mob Seeks to Lynch Negro', 'Man Hunt in Iowa', 'Mob Pursues Colored Man' predicted a lynching without comment; the Minneapolis Journal's subhead called Clark a 'Black Brute'.
The Ottumwa Courier's Kahoka dispatch called Clark 'the fiend' and said he would be 'hung to the nearest tree'.
Kahoka reports before the trial called mob violence 'a dark blot on the county's name' but warned of it if the sentence fell short of death.
The American Citizen, St. Louis Palladium and Iowa State Bystander carried short wire items; the Bystander repeated 'the confessed ravisher'.

info: Assault alleged on the evening of Saturday, July 25, 1903; the mob turned out early Sunday, July 26, and hunted through at least July 28

On the road between Medill and the Hess farm, about two miles west of Kahoka, Mo.; the hunt spread around Kahoka and Keokuk and into southern Iowa (Mt. Sterling, Centerville). Wire stories were datelined Farmington, Iowa.
Frank Clark, alias 'Yellow' Clark, the target of the mob; described as a 'negro', 'dark mulatto' or 'half-breed'
Accused of assaulting (papers say ravishing) Ollie Hess, a white girl of 15 or 17, and cutting her with a knife or razor
'A mob of farmers' from the Kahoka area, called out by fire bells and whistles; also armed posses under Sheriff Arnold and later Sheriffs Hunolt and Davis
